headline: US Posts $1.99 Trillion Budget Gap for 2026 on Spending Rise
author: Yash Roy

paragraphs.text: (Bloomberg) -- The US federal budget deficit widened to nearly $2 trillion for the 2026 fiscal year, serving a fresh reminder of the scale of government borrowing needs and leaving the nation on track for a record high debt burden in coming years.

For the fiscal year through September, the deficit widened to $1.99 trillion, Treasury Department figures showed on Friday. That marks about a 12% increase on the $1.78 trillion gap recorded for last year. Spending rose by more than 5%, to $7.4 trillion, while receipts increased roughly 3%, to $5.4 trillion.

Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent has singled out tariff refunds as a key to the wider deficit, after he touted a narrowing in the gap for 2025. Those payments were tied to the Supreme Court's February ruling invalidating the bulk of President Donald Trump's tariff hikes in his second term. The administration is in the process of constructing a fresh tariff wall via other legislation.

This year marks the fourth straight with a deficit roughly around $2 trillion. The figures suggest the gap was roughly 6% of gross domestic product — an unusually high figure at a time of relatively low unemployment. Officially, the gap narrowed last year, though that was thanks to an accounting measure — the 2025 Republican tax act tightened limits on student loans, and the Treasury booked that as a reduction in 2025 spending.

While Bessent has declared that the US can bend the debt curve down quickly — thanks especially to a faster sustained economic growth rate as the artificial intelligence boom spurs American productivity — many economists, investors and even other senior public officials are skeptical.

International Monetary Fund Managing Director Kristalina Georgieva said Oct. 14 that "growth, of course, helps but it cannot deliver fast enough the necessary adjustments." A counselor to Bessent, the recently appointed David Zervos, took issue with the assessment, saying in comments to CNBC that the IMF has had "messy" forecasts in the past.

Georgieva's predecessor, current European Central Bank President Christine Lagarde, said the same day that the US deficit "needs to be tackled by any country that is, you know, in that particular category." Congressional Budget Office Director Phillip Swagel said on Oct. 8 that it wasn't "plausible" for growth alone to stabilize US debt levels.

The nonpartisan CBO warned in February that US debt as a ratio of gross domestic product was on track to surpass the 106% record set in 1946, just after World War II, by 2030. One gauge of US public debt outstanding surpassed a record $40 trillion last month.
Bessent has vowed to put forward a fiscal consolidation plan, potentially during the lame duck session of Congress if Republicans lose control of either the House or Senate.

Yet in the meantime, Trump keeps suggesting more outlays. He has called for a close to $500 billion increase in defense spending and has also promised $5,000 checks to every American if Republicans maintain control of both chambers of Congress in the midterm elections next month.
